# Roman invasion of Africa (204–201 BC)

The Roman invasion of Carthaginian North Africa in 204–201 BC was the final overseas campaign of the Second Punic War. Commanded by Publius Cornelius Scipio (later Africanus), the expedition crossed from Sicily to land near Utica, established a base at Castra Cornelia, and conducted a sequence of operations that broke Carthage’s alliances, compelled the recall of Hannibal from Italy, and culminated in Rome’s decisive victory at Zama. The campaign’s major actions included Scipio’s night attack on the Carthaginian and Numidian camps near Utica (203 BC), the Battle of the Great Plains (Campi Magni), a pursuit into Numidia leading to the capture of Syphax at Cirta, a contested truce and naval incident off Carthage, Hannibal’s return, and Zama (202 BC). The war ended under a treaty in 201 BC that dismantled Carthage’s overseas power, restricted its navy and war elephants, imposed a heavy indemnity, and recognized Masinissa’s position in Numidia. Ancient accounts by Polybius, Livy, and Appian agree on the campaign’s broad arc while differing on details such as numbers and some terms of the peace; modern scholarship assesses the invasion as decisive in shifting Mediterranean hegemony to Rome and in reordering North African power around Masinissa’s kingdom .

## Background and strategic context

By 205–204 BC, after years of attrition in Italy, Rome’s leadership debated strategy for closing the war. Scipio, elected consul in 205, pressed to carry the fight into Africa, arguing that striking Carthage directly would sever its alliances, force Hannibal’s recall, and bring a decision more quickly than continuing campaigns in Italy. Livy’s narrative emphasizes both political contention in Rome and Scipio’s ambition; he portrays Scipio preparing in Sicily with the intention “not [for] small operations” but to capture or destroy Carthage, while Rome also addressed manpower strains by demanding extraordinary levies from Latin allies . 

The strategic position in Africa was shaped by the Numidian power struggle between Masinissa of the Massylii, who inclined toward Rome, and Syphax of the Masaesyli, closely aligned with Carthage through Hasdrubal Gisco. Masinissa’s mobility and horsemen had already proved valuable to Rome in Hispania; his support would become critical to Scipio’s operations and to the outcome at Zama . Carthage, defending its heartland around Utica and Carthage itself, relied on allied troops (including Celtiberians) and Syphax’s Numidians to counter Roman landings .

## Preparations and logistics

Scipio concentrated forces and ships in Sicily, using Lilybaeum as the principal embarkation port. Livy describes intensive training, recruiting of volunteers, and extraordinary levies demanded from recalcitrant Latin colonies to refill Roman ranks in the war’s later phase . The Roman fleet escorted transports, and naval support proved vital both for the initial landing and for sustaining the base near Utica. Polybius preserves operational details of Scipio’s naval dispositions: when threatened by Carthaginian ships offshore, he moored decked warships side by side, lashed vessels together with masts and yards, and formed a defensive line with transports clustered behind, leaving passages for light craft—an improvised “floating fortification” designed to neutralize enemy maneuver advantage .

## Landing and operations around Utica (204 BC)

Scipio crossed from Sicily and landed near Utica in 204 BC. He established a fortified base on the promontory later known as Castra Cornelia (Latin “Cornelia’s Camp”), opposite Utica and projecting into the sea. Ancient geographic notices and geoarchaeological work place Castra Cornelia on the Kalaat el-Andalous ridge north of Utica, with the Stadiasmus Maris Magni noting a harbor at Castra Cornelia rather than at Utica itself and Caesar describing the ridge’s steep seaward sides and gentler ascent toward Utica . The Roman presence threatened Carthage’s coastal lines and pressured the city to combine forces with Syphax and Hasdrubal Gisco to break Scipio’s position. Initial efforts to take Utica did not succeed, leading Scipio to winter at his base while gathering intelligence and shaping conditions for a decisive blow .

## Campaign of 203 BC

### Night attack near Utica (“Battle of the Camps”)

In early 203 BC, Scipio exploited laxity in the Carthaginian–Numidian camps to mount a night attack by fire against the combined forces of Hasdrubal Gisco and Syphax. Polybius, who emphasizes stratagems and operational audacity, describes Scipio’s choice of arson as a method both unexpected and devastating, producing panic and a rapidly spreading conflagration that destroyed large portions of the enemy camps . Livy gives casualty totals and trophies: tens of thousands killed and thousands captured, numerous standards seized, and several elephants taken or killed, figures he presents to illustrate the attack’s shock effect on Carthaginian morale and cohesion . Appian also situates this action as the turning point that forced Carthage into reactive diplomacy and strategic withdrawal inland .

### Battle of the Great Plains (Campi Magni)

Regrouping after the disaster at the camps, Hasdrubal Gisco and the Numidian leader (often identified as Syphax or his lieutenant) drew up an army on the Great Plains (Campi Magni), a broad inland area west/southwest of Utica. Livy’s account shows Scipio advancing to offer battle and routing the Carthaginian forces, scattering them and opening the way into Numidia . The exact location of the “Great Plains” remains debated, but it is commonly treated as the fertile interior plains of northern Tunisia, consistent with the subsequent pursuit toward Cirta.

### Pursuit into Numidia and capture of Syphax (Cirta)

Scipio detached Gaius Laelius and Masinissa to pursue Syphax north and west into Numidia. They took Cirta—Syphax’s capital—where Syphax was captured and handed over to the Romans; he was transported to Italy and died in captivity at Tibur (modern Tivoli) . The seizure of Cirta consolidated Masinissa’s position and severed Carthage’s most important inland alliance. In Roman narratives, the fall of Cirta also prompts moralizing episodes (e.g., Livy’s version of Sophonisba), but the political outcome is that Numidia became a friendly and increasingly assertive power under Masinissa .

### Diplomacy, truce, and naval incidents

After the Great Plains, Carthage sought negotiations. Livy and Appian recount armistice talks and provisional terms offered by Scipio, including the surrender of prisoners and deserters, evacuation of Italy, Gaul and Spain, reduction of the Carthaginian fleet, and material supplies to Roman forces . During the truce period, a storm drove Roman transports ashore near Carthage, and Carthaginian ships towed several into the harbor—an incident treated by Roman sources as a breach of the armistice. Polybius and Livy present the episode in close connection with heightened naval caution: Scipio had already adopted wall-like mooring tactics against attack, and the contested seizure of stranded transports during truce intensified Roman demands . These incidents hardened positions and helped precipitate the final recall of Hannibal from Italy.

## Recall of Hannibal and the Battle of Zama (202 BC)

Carthage recalled Hannibal after sixteen years of campaigning in Italy. He disembarked, reorganized his forces with remaining Carthaginian troops and African levies, and advanced inland to meet Scipio. Ancient sources present pre-battle negotiations between the two commanders, a feature both Polybius and Livy employ to frame Zama as the war’s decisive confrontation . 

At Zama, Scipio arranged his manipular infantry in three lines with deliberate intervals to channel war elephants, light troops forward to harass and part them, and Roman/Italian cavalry under Gaius Laelius on one wing with Masinissa’s Numidian cavalry on the other. Appian gives approximate Roman infantry strength around 23,000, Roman/Italian cavalry about 1,500, and notes Masinissa’s numerous Numidian horse; he places Hannibal’s cavalry around 4,000 with war elephants in the van (ancient sources generally agree elephants were deployed in front, with some modern estimates giving their number around eighty, though explicit counts vary by source) . As the elephants advanced, Scipio’s intervals and skirmishers diverted many through the lanes; others were blunted by missile fire or by dismounted troopers stabbing at vulnerable points. After a hard infantry fight, Masinissa’s cavalry returned from pursuit and struck Hannibal’s rear, tipping the battle to Rome . 

The site of Zama is contested in modern scholarship. Polybius and Livy refer to Zama, often understood as Zama Regia (near Sidi Abd el Djedidi), while some ancient and modern references place the battle near Naraggara (frequently identified in the El Kef region near modern Sakiet Sidi Youssef). Epigraphic and toponymic evidence attests multiple “Zamas” (e.g., Zama Maior), and the exact battlefield remains debated; the consensus is that it lay in the inland plains south or southwest of Carthage rather than on the coast .

## Treaty of 201 BC and immediate aftermath

Following Zama, Carthage sued for peace. Livy, Polybius, Appian, and Eutropius transmit broadly consistent but not identical terms. Key provisions included: 
- Surrender of all Roman prisoners and deserters, evacuation from Italy, Gaul, and Spain, and renunciation of claims to islands between Italy and Africa . 
- Naval restrictions: Livy reports Carthage was to retain only twenty decked ships, whereas Eutropius gives thirty; all other warships were to be surrendered . 
- Elephant restrictions: destruction of war elephants and prohibition on their future use . 
- Payment of a heavy indemnity, commonly rendered as 10,000 talents (with Eutropius reporting 500,000 pounds of silver) in installments over many years; grain supplies for Roman forces immediately . 
- Foreign-policy constraints: Carthage was forbidden to wage war outside Africa, and later tradition emphasized that even defensive war in Africa would require Roman assent; Rome recognized Masinissa and supported his claims against Carthage’s remaining borderlands . 

Under the settlement, Carthage lost its overseas possessions, ceded its navy, and accepted Roman oversight of external affairs. Masinissa emerged as Rome’s principal client and beneficiary in North Africa, expanding Numidian territory at Carthage’s expense. Scipio celebrated a triumph and received the agnomen “Africanus,” marking the campaign’s political resonance at Rome .

## Forces and tactics

- Roman forces: Scipio’s invasion force was assembled from legions in Sicily and volunteers, with additional levies from Latin allies. At Zama, Appian’s figures suggest roughly 23,000 Roman infantry, c. 1,500 Roman/Italian cavalry, and substantial Numidian cavalry under Masinissa (including detachments under sub-commanders), though exact totals differ in ancient accounts . 
- Carthaginian and Numidian forces: Before 203, Carthage fielded composite forces including Celtiberian infantry and Syphax’s Numidian contingents; at Zama, Hannibal’s army comprised veterans returned from Italy, African levies, and cavalry (c. 4,000 per Appian) with war elephants in front . 
- Naval support: The Roman fleet transported troops and sustained Castra Cornelia. Polybius notes Scipio’s defensive anchoring system, lashing ships into a barrier to resist Carthaginian naval probes and to protect transports . 
- Tactics: The night attack near Utica exemplified Roman use of stratagem (ignis, fire-attack) against a larger coalition force in camp. At Zama, Roman manipular doctrine combined with engineered intervals to dissipate elephant charges, while cavalry under Laelius and Masinissa coordinated to defeat Hannibal’s horse and deliver the decisive envelopment. Ancient narratives stress discipline, flexibility of the manipular system, and the operational value of Numidian cavalry .

Casualty figures vary. Livy supplies high totals for the night attack at Utica; Appian describes very heavy losses at Zama (many thousands killed and captured), but different authors give different numbers; modern historians note the tendency of ancient sources to inflate battlefield counts .

## Chronology and geography (204–201 BC)

- 204 BC: Roman landing near Utica; establishment of Castra Cornelia; initial operations and failed attempt to take Utica; wintering near Utica . 
- Early 203 BC: Night attack burning Carthaginian–Numidian camps near Utica (“Battle of the Camps”) . 
- 203 BC: Battle of the Great Plains (Campi Magni); Roman victory and advance inland . 
- 203 BC: Pursuit into Numidia; capture of Syphax at Cirta; consolidation of Masinissa’s position . 
- Late 203 BC: Truce negotiations; contested naval incident off Carthage involving stranded Roman transports; breakdown of armistice . 
- 202 BC: Hannibal recalled from Italy; Battle of Zama; Roman victory . 
- 201 BC: Peace treaty ratified; Carthage’s navy reduced; indemnity imposed; Masinissa recognized; Scipio’s triumph . 

Place-name correspondences: 
- Utica: ancient port north of Carthage; modern site inland due to delta progradation; harbor likely on the promontory’s northern façade . 
- Castra Cornelia: promontory ridge (Kalaat el-Andalous) north of Utica, associated with Roman camp and harbor facilities . 
- Campi Magni (“Great Plains”): interior plains of northern Tunisia; exact battlefield uncertain . 
- Cirta: Numidian capital; identified with Constantine (Algeria) . 
- Zama/Naraggara: inland sites south/southwest of Carthage; Zama Regia often placed near Sidi Abd el Djedidi; Naraggara commonly identified near the El Kef region; epigraphic attestations include Zama Maior .

## Diplomacy and peace terms

Negotiations in 203–201 BC move through phases: provisional armistice terms after the Great Plains; incidents at sea that Romans treated as violations; the recall of Hannibal; and final talks after Zama. Livy and Appian present Scipio’s demands consistently (prisoners, evacuations, naval reduction, elephant ban, indemnity). Eutropius’ succinct summary preserves variant numbers (e.g., thirty ships rather than twenty, and 500,000 pounds of silver), indicating either different traditions or later simplification . A long-term clause widely noted in modern reference works forbade Carthage from waging war without Roman permission, reinforcing Rome’s intent to neutralize Carthaginian power and elevate Masinissa, whose cavalry had been decisive at Zama and whose kingship Rome now backed .

## Aftermath and significance

The treaty ended Carthage’s overseas empire, restricted its fleet and elephants, and made its foreign policy dependent on Rome. Numidia under Masinissa expanded at Carthage’s expense, becoming a central North African power allied to Rome. Scipio’s triumph and agnomen Africanus symbolized Rome’s ascendancy. Modern overviews of the Second Punic War treat the African campaign as decisive: by forcing Hannibal’s recall, breaking Carthage’s alliances, and winning Zama, Rome secured Mediterranean supremacy and set conditions for the interwar period marked by Masinissa’s encroachments and Carthage’s constrained recovery, culminating decades later in the Third Punic War .

## Sources and historiography

- Polybius, a contemporary Greek historian friendly to Roman elites, privileges operational analysis and typically sober numbers. He extols the night attack near Utica as Scipio’s most daring exploit and details Zama’s tactics (intervals against elephants, cavalry coordination), while also recording treaty terms; his narrative is central for battlefield reconstruction . 
- Livy, writing under Augustus, provides a full annalistic account with speeches and moral exempla. He supplies many specific figures (casualties and trophies at Utica; naval reduction to twenty ships; episodes around Cirta) and preserves theatrical elements of diplomacy and recall; his totals are often higher than Polybius’s and may embed rhetorical amplification . 
- Appian, a Roman imperial historian, offers a continuous Punic Wars narrative. His Zama section gives explicit troop estimates, emphasizes the elephants’ neutralization and cavalry’s decisive return, and outlines the peace terms and Roman ratification process . 
- Eutropius compresses treaty terms into a brief Latin digest with variant numbers; his account helps illustrate the transmission of the settlement’s essentials in late antiquity . 
- Modern scholarship and reference works contextualize the campaign’s significance, the Numidian dimension, and geographic identifications (Utica’s harbor, Castra Cornelia, and Zama loci). Geoarchaeological studies reconstruct the paleo-shoreline around Utica, while epigraphic and toponymic resources attest multiple Zamas (e.g., Zama Maior) and sustain the debate over the Zama/Naraggara battlefield .

[Appian of Alexandria](https://www.livius.org/sources/content/appian/appian-the-punic-wars/appian-the-punic-wars-5/#22)**(c.95-c.165**): one of the most underestimated of all Greek historians, author of a _[Roman History](https://www.livius.org/sources/content/appian/)_ in twenty-four books.

His account of the Punic Wars is fortunately among these better preserved parts. The modern reader will be surprised to learn about its contents, because the conflict we know as the [First Punic War](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/first-punic-war/) is absent (Appian calls it the _[Sicilian War](https://www.livius.org/sources/content/appian/appian-the-wars-on-the-islands-1/)_), and the historian has treated the Spanish and Italian parts of what is now known as the Second Punic War in his books on the _[Spanish Wars](https://www.livius.org/sources/content/appian/appian-the-spanish-wars/)_ and _[Hannibalic War](https://www.livius.org/sources/content/appian/appian-war-against-hannibal/)_. What Appian offers is a description of all Roman military operations in Africa from the final phase of the war against [Hannibal](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/hannibal-3-barca/) until the final pacification by the emperor [Augustus](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/augustus/). There is an appendix on the [Numidian](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/numidia/) Wars.

The translation was made by Horace White; notes by Jona Lendering.

There are two systems to divide the _Punic Wars_: in 136 sections or 20 chapters. On these webpages, the text is divided into sections; the following table shows the division into chapters.

4.title: Appian, The Punic Wars 9
4.content:
**[Appian of Alexandria](https://www.livius.org/sources/content/appian/) (c.95-c.165):** one of the most underestimated of all Greek historians, author of a _[Roman History](https://www.livius.org/sources/content/appian/)_ in twenty-four books.

Although only Appian's books on the [Roman Civil Wars](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Appian/home.html) survive in their entirety, large parts of the other books, devoted to Rome's foreign wars, have also come down to us. The parts on the [Punic wars](https://www.livius.org/sources/content/appian/appian-the-punic-wars/), the [wars in Iberia](https://www.livius.org/sources/content/appian/appian-the-spanish-wars/), and the [Mithridatic Wars](https://www.livius.org/sources/content/appian/appian-the-mithridatic-wars/) are very important historical sources. This is also true for Appian's account of the Third Punic War, the second part of the book presented on these pages, which is one of our main sources for this conflict.

Because these texts have to be reconstructed from several medieval manuscripts, not all editions of Appian's account of Rome's foreign wars are numbered in the same way. On these pages, the separate units of a book are counted strictly chronologically.

The translation was made by Horace White; notes by Jona Lendering.

* * *

### The Second Punic War (cont'd)

[41]Scipio note had about 23,000 foot and 1,500 Italian and Roman horse. He had as allies [Massinissa](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/massinissa/) with a large number of [Numidian](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/numidia/) horse, and another prince, named Dacamas, with 1,600 horse. He drew up his infantry, like those of [Hannibal](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/hannibal-3-barca/), in three lines. He placed all his cohorts in straight lines with open spaces so that the cavalry might readily pass between them. In front of each cohort he stationed men armed with heavy stakes two cubits long, mostly shod with iron, for the purpose of assailing the oncoming elephants by hand, as with catapult bolts. He ordered these and the other foot-soldiers to avoid the impetus of these beasts by turning aside and continually hurling javelins at them, and by darting around them to hamstring them whenever they could. In this way Scipio disposed his infantry.

He stationed his Numidian horse on his wings because they were accustomed to the sight and smell of elephants. As the Italian horse were not so, he placed them all in the rear, ready to charge through the intervals of the foot-soldiers when the latter should have checked the first onset of the elephants. To each horseman was assigned an attendant armed with plenty of darts with which to ward off the attack of these beasts. In this way was his cavalry disposed. Laelius note commanded the right wing and Octavius the left.

In the middle both Hannibal and himself took their stations, out of respect for each other, each having a body of horse in order to send reinforcements wherever they might be needed. Of these Hannibal had 4,000 and Scipio 2,000, besides the 300 Italians whom he had armed in [Sicily](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/sicily/).

[42]When everything was ready each one rode up and down encouraging his soldiers. Scipio, in the presence of his army, invoked the gods, whom the [Carthaginians](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/carthage/) had offended by their frequent violation of treaties. He told the soldiers not to think of the numbers of the enemy but of their own valor, by which aforetime these same enemies, in even greater numbers, had been overcome in this same country. If fear, anxiety, and doubt oppress those who have hitherto been victorious, how much more, he said, must these feelings weigh upon the vanquished. Thus did Scipio encourage his forces and console them for their inferiority in numbers.

Hannibal reminded his men of what they had done in Italy, their great and brilliant victories won, not over Numidians, but over those who were all Italians, and throughout Italy. He pointed out, in plain sight, the smallness of the enemy's force, and exhorted them not to show themselves inferior to a less numerous body in their own country. Each general magnified to his own men the consequences of the coming engagement. Hannibal said that the battle would decide the fate of Carthage and all Africa; if vanquished, they would be enslaved forthwith, if victorious, they would have universal supremacy hereafter. Scipio said that there was no safe refuge for his men if they were vanquished, but if victorious there would be a great increase of the Roman power, a rest from their present labors, a speedy return home, and glory forever after.

[43]Having thus exhorted their men they joined battle. Hannibal ordered the trumpet to sound, and Scipio responded in like manner. The elephants began the fight decked out in fearful [panoply](https://www.livius.org/articles/objects/panoply/)and urged on with goads by their riders. The Numidian horse flying around them incessantly thrust darts into them. Being wounded and put to flight and having become unmanageable, their drivers took them out of the combat. This is what happened to the elephants on both wings. Those in the center trampled down the Roman infantry, who were not accustomed to that kind of fighting and were not able to avoid or to pursue them easily on account of their heavy armor, until Scipio brought up the Italian cavalry, who were in the rear and more lightly armed, and ordered them to dismount from their frightened horses, and run around and stab the elephants. He was himself the first to dismount and wound the front-tramping elephant. The others were encouraged by his example, and they inflicted so many wounds upon the elephants that these also withdrew.

[44]The field being cleared of these beasts the battle was now waged by men and horses only. The Roman right wing, where Laelius commanded, put the opposing Numidians to flight, and Massinissa struck down their prince, Massathes, with a dart, but Hannibal quickly came to their rescue and restored the line of battle. On the left wing, where Octavius commanded and where the hostile Celts and Ligurians were stationed, a doubtful battle was going on. Scipio sent the tribune Thermus note thither with a reinforcement of picked men, but Hannibal, after rallying his left wing, flew to the assistance of the Ligurians and Celts, bringing up at the same time his second line of Carthaginians and Africans. Scipio, perceiving this, brought his second line in opposition. When the two greatest generals of the world thus met, in hand to hand fight, there was, on the part of the soldiers of each, a brilliant emulation and reverence for their commanders, and no lack of zeal on either side in the way of sharp and vehement fighting and cheering.

[45]As the battle was long and undecided, the two generals had compassion on their tired soldiers, and rushed upon each other in order to bring it to a more speedy decision. They threw their javelins at the same time. Scipio pierced Hannibal's shield. Hannibal hit Scipio's horse. The horse, smarting from the wound, threw Scipio over backwards. He quickly mounted another and again hurled a dart at Hannibal, but missed him and struck another horseman near him.

At this juncture, Massinissa, hearing of the crisis, came up, and the Romans seeing their general not only serving as a commander but fighting also as a common soldier, fell upon the enemy more vehemently than before, routed them, and pursued them in flight. Nor could Hannibal, who rode by the side of his men and besought them to make a stand and renew the battle, prevail upon them to do so. Therefore, despairing of these, he turned to the Italians who had come with him, and who were still in reserve and not demoralized. These he led into the fight, hoping to fall upon the Romans in disorderly pursuit. But they perceived his intention, and speedily called one another back from the pursuit and restored the line of battle. As their horse were no longer with them and they were destitute of missiles, they now fought sword in hand in close combat. Great slaughter ensued and innumerable wounds, mingled with the shouts of the combatants and the groans of the dying, until, finally, the Romans routed these also and put them to flight. Such was the brilliant issue of this engagement.

![Image 1: 
[Much of my site will be useless to you if you've got the images turned off!]
	](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/Images/Utility/empty.gif)

(Vol.IV) Polybius 

 The Histories
----------------------------------

[p429](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) Fragments of Book XIV
-------------------------------------------------------------------

### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) I.Affairs of Greece

[11a](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) Perhaps it is true that in all Olympiads the syllabus of events arrests the attention of the reader, owing to their number and importance, the actions of the whole world being brought under one point of view. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But I think the events of this Olympiad (CXLIV) will have a peculiar power of doing this. For in the first place it was during this Olympiad that the wars in Italy and Africa were brought to an end, wars the final outcome of which who will not be curious to learn? [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For everyone naturally, although he may completely accept our account of particular action and speeches, still always longs to know the end. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Besides this, the political tendencies of the kings were clearly revealed during these years. For all that had been hitherto a matter of gossip about them now became clearly known to everyone, even to those who were not at all disposed to be curious. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For this reason, as I wish to give such an account of the facts as their [p431](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)importance deserves, I have not comprised the events of two years in one Book as was my practice in previous cases.

### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) II.Scipio in Africa

[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The consuls, then, were engaged in these matters, but Publius Scipio, who was in winter quarters in Africa, hearing that the Carthaginians were getting a fleet ready, occupied himself in making his own naval preparations, but continued to prosecute none the less the siege of Utica. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Nor did he entirely abandon his hope of winning over Syphax, but sent frequent messages to him, their armies being at no great distance from each other, feeling sure of indu­cing him to abandon the Carthaginian alliance. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He thought it indeed not at all unlikely that he had already grown tired of the girl⁠[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/14*.html#note1) for whose sake he had chosen the cause of the Carthaginians, and tired generally of his friendship for Phoenicians, as Scipio well knew the natural tendency of the Numidians to grow disgusted with what pleased them and how lightly they always break their faith to gods and men alike. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)At present his mind was much distracted and agitated by various apprehensions, as he feared an attack owing to the enemy's superiority in numbers, and he gladly availed himself of the following occasion when it offered itself. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Some of his messengers to Syphax reported that the Carthaginians in their winter camp had made their huts from all kinds of wood and branches without any mixture of earth, [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)that the first Numidians to arrive had constructed theirs with [p433](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)reeds, while the others who kept joining the army from the cities had used nothing but branches for the present, some of them being encamped inside but most outside [•](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/secondary/SMIGRA*/Vallum.html)the trench and palisade. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio, therefore, thinking that an attempt to fire the camp would be a complete surprise for the enemy and very serviceable to himself, began to take the necessary measures. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Syphax in his communications with Scipio always kept harking back to the opinion that the Carthaginians ought to evacuate Italy and the Romans do the same as regards Africa, each nation continuing to occupy the points they held between these two countries. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio had previously refused entirely to listen to this proposal, but he now ordered his messengers to throw out slight hints to the Numidian prince that the attainment of this end was not beyond the bounds of possibility. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Syphax was very much relieved in consequence and became much more disposed than he had been to engage in parleys, [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)the consequence being that the messengers became more numerous and their visits more frequent, some of them at times spending several days in the hostile camp without any objection being made. [13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio on such occasions used to send in the company of his envoys certain expert observers and certain of his officers, looking mean and dirty fellows, disguised as they were in the habit of slaves, with the object of exploring and inspecting undisturbed the approaches and the entrances of both camps. [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For there were two of them, one occupied by Hasdrubal with thirty thousand foot and three thousand horse, and another at a distance of [•](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)ten stades belonging to the Numidians and containing about ten thousand horse and fifty thousand foot. [p435](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[15](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The latter was the easiest to attack and the huts very suitable for setting on fire, since the Numidians, as I just said, used neither wood nor earth for their huts, but only reeds and matting.

[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)As soon as there were signs of the approach of spring, Scipio having now completed all the inquiries necessary for the above design against the enemy, launched his ships and constructed siege-machines to place on them as if he were about to blockade Utica from the sea. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)With his infantry, who numbered about two thousand, he again occupied the hill situated above the town and spared no expense in fortifying this hill and digging a moat round it, giving the enemy the idea that he did so for the purpose of the siege, but in reality desiring to secure himself from possible danger on the day of his enterprise; for he feared lest when his legions had left their camp the garrison of Utica might venture on a sortie, and falling on the camp, which was close by, besiege the force left to defend it. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)While making these preparations he sent a message to Syphax to inquire, on the supposition that the proposed terms met with his own approval, if they would also be agreeable to the Carthaginians and if they could be trusted not to say again that they would further consider before accepting what he was ready to concede. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He also instructed his envoys not to return to him before receiving an answer to this question. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When they arrived and Syphax had received the message, he felt convinced that Scipio was determined to conclude the treaty, both because the envoys had told him they would not return without [p437](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)an answer and because of the anxiety shown to make sure of the consent of the Carthaginians. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)So he sent off at once to Hasdrubal informing him of what had occurred and begging him to accept peace, while he himself passed his time at his ease and allowed the Numidians who kept on joining him to encamp outside his fortified camp. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio pretended to do the same, but as a fact was making every possible preparation for his attack. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When Syphax had once been instructed by the Carthaginians to conclude the peace, and overjoyed at this, spoke to the envoys on the matter, they at once left for their own camp to tell Scipio the result of the king's action. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Roman commander, on hearing of it, lost no time in sending other envoys to announce to Syphax that Scipio approved of peace and was earnestly working for it, but that members of the council were of a different opinion, maintaining that matters should rest as they were. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The envoys went to Syphax and informed him to this effect. [13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio dispatched this embassy in order not to appear to have broken the truce if, while formal negotiations for peace were still in progress, he committed any hostile act. [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But after having made this declaration he considered that whatever happened no one could find fault with his conduct.

[3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Syphax, on hearing this, was no little vexed as he had made up his mind that peace was assured, but he now met Hasdrubal and communicated to him the message he had received from the Romans. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After much discussion of it they fell to considering [p439](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)how they should now deal with the situation, being very far both in their apprehensions and designs from any suspicion of which was actually about to happen. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For they never had the least thought of taking any precaution for their security or of the likelihood of any disaster, but they were very eager and anxious to take some active steps and to challenge the enemy to battle on level ground. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio, in the meanwhile, by his preparations and the orders he issued gave his soldiery to understand that he was about to make an attempt to seize Utica by surprise, [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but summoning the ablest and most trusty of his tribunes about midday, and disclosing his plan ordered them to get their supper early and then lead the legions out of the camp, after the trumpeters had all sounded the retreat as usual. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For it is the custom among the Romans at supper-time for the trumpeters and buglers to sound their instruments outside the general's tent as a signal that it is time to set the night-watches at their several stations. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After this, calling the spies whom he used to send to the enemy's camps, he questioned them closely and compared the accounts they gave of the approaches and entrances of the camps, letting Massanissa decide, and following his advice owing to his personal knowledge of the ground.

[4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When all was in readiness for his present enterprise, he left a sufficient body of troops suitable for the purpose to guard the camp and advanced with the rest of his army just at the end of the first watch, the enemy being at a distance of sixty stades. [p441](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When towards the end of the third watch he approached them he placed half of his legionaries and all the Numidians under the command of Gaius Laelius and Massanissa with orders to attack the camp of Syphax, exhorting them to behave like brave men and to do nothing rashly, as they well knew that the more the darkness in night attacks hinders and impedes the sight, the more must one supply the place of actual vision by skill and daring. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He himself, with the rest of his army, advanced to attack Hasdrubal. He had made up his mind not to deliver his attack before Laelius had set fire to the other hostile camp, and, therefore, this being his purpose, marched at a slow pace. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Laelius and Massanissa dividing their forces into two attacked the enemy simultaneously. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The huts having been, as I stated above, almost specially constructed for the purpose of catching fire, once the front ranks of the Romans had set the fire alight it spread at once over the first row, and made the evil irremediable owing to the closeness of the huts to each other and the quantity of the fuel it fed on. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Laelius remained to cover the operation, and Massanissa, knowing the places by which those who were trying to escape from the flames would have to pass, stationed his own men at those posts. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Absolutely none of the Numidians had any suspicion of the actual fact, not even Syphax, but they all supposed that the camp had caught fire by accident. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)So that suspecting [p443](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)nothing, some of them aroused from sleep and others surprised while still drinking and carousing, they rushed out of their huts. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Many were trampled to death in the passages that led out of the camp, and many others were caught by the flames and consumed, while all those who escaped from the fire fell into the midst of the enemy and perished without knowing what was happening to them or what they were doing.

[5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Meanwhile the Carthaginians, when they saw the strength of the fire and the volume of flame that rose to the sky, thinking that the Numidian camp had caught fire by accident, rushed some of them to give assistance, while all the rest, flocking out of their camp unarmed, stood in front of it in a state of terror at what was taking place. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio, now that all had gone as well as he could have wished, fell upon those who had come out. Killing some and pursuing others he set their huts also on fire, with the result that the scene of conflagration and general destruction I have just described in the case of the Numidian camp was reproduced in that of the Phoenicians. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Hasdrubal at once entirely desisted from any attempt to extinguish the fire, as he knew now from what had befallen him that the calamity that had befallen the Numidians also was not, as they had supposed, the result of chance but was due to the initiative and daring of the enemy. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He now thought but of saving himself, and there was very little hope left of even doing this. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For the fire spread with great rapidity, and soon covered the whole area of the camp, the passages of which were full of horses, mules, and men, some half-dead [p445](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)and consumed by the flames, and some frenzied and beside themselves, so that even those ready to make a bold effort were prevented by these obstacles, and owing to the confusion and disturbance there was no hope of safety. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Syphax, too, and the other officers were in the same plight. The two generals, however, managed to escape with a small body of horse, but of the rest those thousands and thousands of men, horses, and mules met with an unhappy and miserable end in the flames, [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)while some of the men trying to escape the fury of the fire died a disgraceful and dishonourable death at the hands of the enemy, cut down as they were naked, not only without their arms but without their clothes. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)In a word the whole place was filled with wailing and confused cries, panic fear, strange noises, and above all raging fire and flames that overbore all resistance, things any one of which would be sufficient to strike terror into a human heart, and how much more this extraordinary combination of them all. [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)So it is not possible to find any other disaster which even if exaggerated could be compared with this, so much did it exceed in horror all previous events. [15](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Therefore of all the brilliant exploits performed by Scipio this seems to me the most splendid and most adventurous....

[6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But when day dawned, and the enemy had all either perished or were in headlong flight, Scipio exhorted his officers and at once started in pursuit. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Carthaginian commander at first remained where he was, although he had received notice of the approach of the Romans; it was his confidence in the strength of the town in which he was that made him act thus. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But afterwards, when he saw that [p447](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)the inhabitants of the place were disaffected, the prospect of being attacked by Scipio dismayed him and he continued his flight with all those who had escaped, and who consisted of not less than five hundred horse and about two thousand foot. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Upon this the inhabitants with one accord surrendered at discretion to the Romans. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio spared them, but gave up two of the neighbouring towns to his soldiers to pillage and after this returned to his original camp.

[6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Carthaginians, now that the prospect of success in their original design had been reversed, were deeply dejected. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For they had hoped to shut in the Romans on the cape adjacent to Utica, which they made their winter quarters, besieging them by land with their armies and by sea with their navy and had made all preparations for this purpose; so that now when by a strange and unexpected disaster they had not only been obliged to abandon to the enemy the command of the open country but expected that at any moment they themselves and their city would be in imminent peril, they became thoroughly dismayed and faint-hearted. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The situation, however, demanded that they should take precautions and deliberate as to the future, and when the senate assembled it was full of perplexity and the most divergent and tumultuary suggestions abounded. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Some held that they should send to Hannibal and recall him from Italy, their only remaining hope being in that general and his army, [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)others proposed sending an embassy to Scipio to ask for a truce and speak to him about terms of peace, while others said they should pluck up courage and [p449](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)communicate with Syphax, [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)who had retired to Abba quite near by, and collect the troops who had escaped from the disaster. This was the counsel which finally prevailed.

[13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Carthaginians, then, began to assemble their forces, dispatching Hasdrubal to do so, and at the same time sent to Syphax entreating him to help them and to remain firm to his first engagements, assuring him that Hasdrubal would at once join him with his army. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Roman general both occupied himself with preparations for the siege of Utica and now, on hearing that Syphax remained faithful and that the Carthaginians were again collecting an army, led out his own forces and encamped before that city. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He also at the same time distributed the booty, but sent about their business the merchants who were making too good an affair of it; for as their recent success had made them form a rosy picture of the future, the soldiers attached no value to their actual booty and were very ready to dispose of it to the merchants for a song.

[4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Numidian prince and his friends had at first decided to continue their retreat and seek their homes, [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but when they were met near Abba by the Celtiberians who had been hired by the Carthaginians and who numbered over four thousand, the reliance they placed on this additional force made them halt and pluck up a little courage. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)And when at the same time the young girl, who was, as I have said, the daughter of the general, Hasdrubal, and wife of Syphax, begged and entreated him to remain and not desert the Carthaginians at such a critical [p451](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)time, the Numidian prince suffered himself to be persuaded and yielded to her prayers. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Celtiberians contributed also not a little to inspire the Carthaginians with hope. For instead of four thousand it was announced that they were ten thousand, and that their personal courage and their armament rendered them invincible in the field. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)These reports and the vulgar gossip of the rabble raised so much the spirits of the Carthaginians that their confidence in being able to take the field once more against the enemy was redoubled. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Finally in thirty days they encamped and entrenched themselves on the so‑called Great Plain together with the Numidians and Celtiberians, the whole force numbering not less than thirty thousand.

[8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)When the news reached the Roman camp, Scipio at once prepared to advance against them, and after giving the necessary orders to the land and sea forces besieging Utica, he set out on his march, his whole force being in light marching order. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)On the fifth day he reached the Great Plain, and on approaching the enemy encamped for the first day on a hill at a distance of thirty stades from them, [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)but on the next day came down from the hill, and pla­cing his cavalry in front drew up his army at a distance of seven stades from the Carthaginians. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)After remaining where they were for the two subsequent days and making trial of their strength by some slight skirmishing, on the fourth day both generals deliberately advanced their forces and arrayed them for battle. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio simply followed the usual Roman practice of pla­cing the maniples of hastati in front, behind them the principes, and hindmost of all the [p453](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)triarii. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He stationed his Italian cavalry on his right and the Numidians with Massanissa on the left. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Syphax and Hasdrubal placed the Celtiberians in the centre opposite the Roman maniples, the Numidians on the left, and the Carthaginians on the right. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)At the first encounter the Numidians gave way before the Italian horse and the Carthaginians before Massanissa, their courage having been broken by previous defeats, but the Celtiberians fought bravely holding out against the Romans. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For they neither had any hope of safety in flight owing to their ignorance of the country, nor could they expect to be spared if made prisoners, owing to their treachery to Scipio in thus coming to fight in the service of Carthage against the Romans in spite of his never having been guilty of any acts of hostility to them during his Spanish campaigns. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But when the wings gave way they were soon surrounded by the principes and triarii and cut to pieces where they stood except quite a few. [12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Thus perished the Celtiberians after proving of the greatest service to the Carthaginians not only in the battle but in the flight. [13](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For if the Romans had not met with this obstacle, but had directly pursued the fugitives, very few of the enemy would have escaped. [14](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But as it was, owing to this stand made by the Celtiberians, Syphax with his cavalry made his way safely back home and Hasdrubal also with the survivors of his force reached Carthage.

p455[9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The Roman general, as soon as he had arranged about the disposal of the booty and prisoners, summoned the council to deliberate as to what should be done next. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)It was decided that Scipio with a part of his army should remain and go round to the several cities, while Laelius and Massanissa with the Numidians and a portion of the Roman legions should follow up Syphax and not give him time to stop and prepare for resistance. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Having come to this decision they separated, these two going after Syphax with the troops I mentioned and the general visiting the towns, some of which surrendered voluntarily to the Romans out of fear, while he besieged and stormed others. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The whole country indeed was inclined for a change, as the people had been constantly exposed to hardship and excessive taxation owing to the long duration of the war in Spain.

[6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)In Carthage itself the disorder had been serious enough previously, but now the city was still more deeply disturbed, and it seemed that after this second heavy blow they had lost all confidence in themselves. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But nevertheless the advice of those who were thought to be the boldest spirits in the senate was to sail with the fleet against the besiegers of Utica and attempt to raise the siege and engage the enemy's fleet, which was unprepared for an encounter. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)They also demanded that Hannibal should be summoned to return and that resource put to the test without any delay. Both these [p457](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)measures, they said, offered, as far as could be reasonably judged, great chances of saving the country. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But others maintained that the time for these steps was past, and that they must now strengthen the city and prepare for a siege. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For if they only preserved concord, chance would afford many opportunities. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)They also advised them to take the question of peace into consideration, and to decide on what terms and by what means they could be delivered from the present evils. [11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)There were several debates on these proposals and finally they adopted them all. [10](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)As soon as the vote had been taken, those senators who were to sail for Italy proceeded directly from the senate-house to sea, and the admiral went straight on board his ship. The remainder made it their business to see to the defences of the city and met frequently to discuss points of detail.

[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio's camp was now full of booty, as he met with no resistance but all gave way to him no matter what he attempted, and he decided to send off the great part of the booty to his original camp, and taking with him his army thus lightened to seize on the entrenched position before Tunis and to encamp in full view of Carthage. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)For this he thought would be the most effective means of striking the Carthaginians with terror and dismay. The Carthaginians had got ready in a few days the crews and stores for their ships and were about to put to sea to execute their purpose, when Scipio arrived at Tunis and upon its garrison taking to flight occupied the place. [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Tunis is situated at a distance of about 120 stades from Carthage, and is visible from nearly the whole town. As I have [p459](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)previously stated, both nature and art have contributed to render it a very strong place. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Just as the Romans had encamped there the Carthaginian fleet was putting to sea on its way to Utica. [7](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Scipio when he saw the enemy under way was much disturbed, as he feared that something untoward might happen to his own fleet, since no one expected to be attacked or had made any preparations for such a contingency. [8](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)He, therefore, at once broke up his camp and marched hastily to the help of his own people. [9](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Finding that his warships were well provided with facilities for supporting moving forward siege-machines, and in general for all siege operations, but were quite unprepared for a naval action, while the enemy's fleet had during the whole winter been equipping for this very purpose, he abandoned any idea of advancing and offering battle, but anchoring his warships in a line placed round them the transports three or four deep, and then taking down the masts and yards lashed the transports securely to each other with these, leaving a small interval for dispatch-boats to pass in and out.

### [](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/) III.Affairs of Egypt since B.C.213⁠[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/14*.html#note2)

[11](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Polybius in his fourteenth book says that Philo was the flatterer of Agathocles, the son of Oenanthe and the companion of Ptolemy Philopator....

⁠[3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/14*.html#note3)[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Polybius in his fourteenth book tells us that there were many portraits in Alexandrian temples of Cleino, the cupbearer of Ptolemy Philadelphus, [p461](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)representing her clothed only in a chiton and holding a rhyton. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)"And are not some of the finest houses," he says, called Myrtion's, Mnesis's, and Potheine's? [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)But what were Mnesis and Potheine but flute-players and Myrtio one of the professional and vulgar mimae? [5](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)And was not Ptolemy Philopator the slave of the courtesan Agathocleia, who overturned the whole kingdom?"....

[12](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Perhaps some of my readers will wonder why while elsewhere I dealt with the successive events of each year separately, in the case of Egypt alone I give on the present occasion a narrative of occurrences there extending over a considerable period. [2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)The reason of this I may state as follows. [3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Ptolemy Philopator, of whom I am now talking, after the termination of the war for Coele-Syria abandoned entirely the path of virtue and took to a life of dissipation such as I have just described. [4](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)Late in his reign he was forced by circumstances into the war I have mentioned, a war which, apart from the mutual savagery and lawlessness of the combatants, contained nothing worthy of note, no pitched battle, no sea-fight, no siege. [6](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/)It, therefore, struck me that my narrative would be easier both for me to write and for my readers to follow if I performed this part of my task not by merely alluding every year to small events not worth serious attention, but by giving once for all a life-like picture so to speak of this king's character.

* * *

The Loeb Editor's Notes:
------------------------

[1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/14*.html#ref1) Sophonisba, daughter of Hasdrubal and granddaughter of Gesco.

❦

[2](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/14*.html#ref2) From [Athen.VI. 251 C](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Athenaeus/6D*.html#p135).

❦

[3](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/14*.html#ref3) From Athen. XIII 756 C.

7.title: Livy, Periochae 26-30 - Livius
7.content:
**Titus Livius** or **Livy** (59 BCE - 17 CE): Roman historian, author of the authorized version of the history of the Roman republic.

A large part of [Livy](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/livy/)'s _History of Rome since the Foundation_ is now lost, but fortunately we have an excerpt, called the _[Periochae](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/livy/livy-the-periochae/)_, which helps us reconstruct the general scope. This translation was made by Jona Lendering.

* * *

### From Book 26

[26.1][211 BCE] [Hannibal](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/hannibal-3-barca/) built his camp at the third milestone from Rome, near the Anio.

[26.2]He personally came up to the [Porta Capena](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/rome/rome-photos/rome-porta-capena/)note with two thousand cavalry, to inspect the city's lie.

[26.3]And when for three days the battle lines on both sides had been ready, a tempest broke off the engagement; when Hannibal had returned to his camp, tranquility returned.

[26.4][Capua](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/capua/) was captured by [consuls](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/consul/) Quintus Fulvius and Appius Claudius.

[26.5]The Campanian leaders killed themselves with poison.

[26.6]When the Campanian [senators](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/senate/) had been tied to the stakes to be decapitated, consul Quintus Fulvius received a letter from the Senate, in which he was ordered to be merciful, but he kept it in the fold [of his toga], and before he had read it, he had already ordered that the law was to be applied, and the executions had already taken place.

[26.7]When at the elections the people were asked who wanted the Spanish command and nobody dared to accept it, Publius [Cornelius] Scipio (the son of the Publius who had fallen in Hispania), announced that he would go; and having been sent by the people's vote and general agreement, he captured [New Carthage](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/carthago-nova-cartagena/), and although he was only twenty-four, he[](https://www.livius.org/sources/content/livy/livy-periochae-26-30/)appeared to be a son of a god, because from the moment he had accepted the toga, he was every day in the [temple of [Jupiter](https://www.livius.org/articles/religion/zeus/) on the] Capitol, and often, a serpent had been seen in the bed room of his mother.

[26.8]It note also contains accounts of the events on [Sicily](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/sicily/), [210] a treaty of friendship with the [Aetolians](https://www.livius.org/articles/misc/aetolian-league/), and war against the Acarnanians and king [Philip](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/philip-v/) of [Macedonia](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/macedonia/).

### From Book 27

[27.1]Near Herdonea, [proconsul](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/proconsul/) Gnaeus Fulvius was defeated with his army by Hannibal.

[27.2]Consul [[Marcus](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/claudius-marcellus/)] [Claudius Marcellus](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/claudius-marcellus/) fought with more success against the same opponent at Numistro.

[27.3]Hannibal retreated under cover of the night.

[27.4]Marcellus pursued him, and inflicted damage upon the retreating army, until Hannibal engaged.

[27.5]In the first battle, Hannibal was superior, but Marcellus in the second.

[27.6][209] Benefiting from treachery, consul Fabius Maximus the Elder recovered [Tarentum](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/tarentum/).

[27.7][208] When consuls [Marcus] Claudius Marcellus and Titus Quinctius Crispinus, on a reconnaissance mission, had advanced from their camp, they were surrounded by Hannibal in an ambush.

[27.8]Marcellus was killed, Crispinus escaped.

[27.9]The [censors](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/censor/) celebrated the _[lustrum](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/lustrum/)_ ceremony.

[27.10]137,108 citizens were registered. From this number, it is clear how many members of the Roman people unfavorable Fortune had carried away in so many defeats.

[27.11][209] In Hispania, near Baecula, Scipio engaged and defeated [Hasdrubal](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/hasdrubal-3-barca/) and Hamilcar.

[27.12]Among those who had been captured was an extraordinary beautiful boy of regal birth, who was sent to his uncle [Massinissa](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/massinissa/), with other presents.

[27.13][207] Hasdrubal, who crossed the Alps with a new army to join Hannibal, was defeated with fifty-six thousand men, and five thousand four hundred were captured, under the command of consul Marcus Livius, but no less by consul Claudius Nero, who, when he opposed Hannibal, left his camp in such fashion that he deceived his enemy, set out with an elite force, and overpowered Hasdrubal.

[27.14]It note also contains an account of the successful wars of Publius [Cornelius] Scipio in Hispania and [praetor](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/praetor/) Publius Sulpicius against [Philip](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/philip-v/)[V of Macedonia] and the [Achaeans](https://www.livius.org/articles/misc/achaean-league/).

### From Book 28

[28.1][207 BCE] It note tells about successes against the [Carthaginians](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/carthage/) in Hispania by Silanus, deputy of Scipio, and Scipio's brother Lucius; and by [proconsul](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/proconsul/) Sulpicius and king [Attalus](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/attalus-i-soter/) [I Soter] of Asia, his ally, against king Philip of Macedonia, on behalf of the Aetolians.

[28.2]When a triumph was decreed for [consuls](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/consul/) Marcus Livius and Claudius Nero, Livius, in whose [province](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/province-roman/) that battle was won, rode in a chariot with four horses, and Nero, who had come to the province of his colleague to help him win the victory, followed him on horseback; but in this fashion, he received more glory and respect, because he had done more in the war than his colleague.

[28.3]The fire in the temple of Vesta went out due to the neglect by one of the Virgins, who did not keep watch over it; she was scourged.

[28.4][206] After completely shutting out the enemies and occupying the whole of Hispania, Publius [Cornelius] Scipio recovered the province an finally defeated the Carthaginians in the fourteenth year of the war, and in the fifth after his arrival. From [Tarraco](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/tarraco-tarragona/), he crossed to Africa and concluded a treaty with [Syphax](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/syphax/), king of the Massylians.note

[28.5][Hasdrubal](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/hasdrubal-4/), the son of [Gesco](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/gesco/), dined with him on the same bed.

[28.6]In New Carthage, Scipio organized a [gladiatorial](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/gladiator/) contest to commemorate his father and uncle. But no gladiators took part: the fighters were men who descended into the arena to honor their commander or accept a challenge. Two princes, brothers, contested the possession of a kingdom.

[28.7]When the town of Gisia was besieged, the citizens killed their children and wives on a pyre they had constructed, and threw themselves into the fire.

[28.8]A rebellion broke out in a part of the army while Scipio himself was ill; when he recovered, he suppressed it and forced the [remaining] Spanish nations into surrender.

[28.9]He also concluded a treaty of friendship with king [Massinissa](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/massinissa/) of the [Numidians](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/numidia/), who promised him help when he should cross to Africa, and he also made friends with the people of Gades after the departure of [Mago](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/mago-barca/), who had been ordered to go to Italy. Scipio returned to Rome and was made consul.

[28.10][205] He asked permission to go to Africa, but Quintus Fabius Maximus opposed this, and Scipio therefore received [Sicily](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/sicily/) and permission to go to Africa if he thought this was for the benefit of the state.

[28.11][Hamilcar](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/hamilcar-2-barca/)'s son Mago spent the winter on the smaller Balearic island, and crossed to Italy.

### From Book 29

[29.1]Gaius Laelius, sent by Scipio from Sicily to Africa, brought back enormous booty and gave Scipio Massinissa's messages, in which he complained that he had not yet sent his army to Africa.

[29.2]When Indebilis provoked a war in Hispania, it ended with a Roman victory; he himself was killed in action, and Mandonius was handed over by his relatives when the Romans asked for it.

[29.3]Mago, who was at Albingaunum in Liguria, received many soldiers and money to hire auxiliaries, and was ordered to join [Hannibal](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/hannibal-3-barca/).

[29.4]Scipio crossed from Sicily to Bruttium and recaptured Locri by putting its Carthaginian garrison to flight and routing Hannibal.

[29.5]A peace treaty was concluded with Philip [V of Macedonia].

[29.6][204] In accordance with an oracle found in the Sibylline books, which stated that a foreign invader would be expelled if the Idaean Mother note had been brought to Rome, the Idaean Mother was brought to Rome from the [Phrygian](https://www.livius.org/articles/people/phrygians/) town [Pessinus](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/pessinus-ballihisar/).

[29.7]She was given to the Romans by king [Attalus](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/attalus-i-soter/) [I Soter] of Asia.

[29.8]According to the natives, the Mother of the gods was a stone.

[29.9]Because the oracle had ordered that the deity had to be received and consecrated by the best man, she was received by Publius [Cornelius] Scipio Nasica (son of the Gnaeus who had perished in Hispania), who was judged by the [Senate](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/senate/) to be the best man, although he was young and had not even reached the [quaestorship](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/quaestor/).

[29.10]The Locrians sent envoys to Rome to complain about the shocking behavior of Pleminius, who had confiscated the money of Prosepina, and had outraged their children and wives.

[29.11]In chains, he was sent to Rome, where he died in jail.

[29.12]When a false rumor concerning proconsul Publius [Cornelius] Scipio, who was on Sicily, circulated in the city, concerning his life in luxury, the Senate sent envoys to investigate the truth of the rumor; Scipio was cleared of the accusation and with the Senate's permission, he crossed to Africa.

[29.13]Syphax, who had married a daughter of Hasdrubal, son of Gesco, renounced his friendship with Scipio.

[29.14]King Massinissa of the Massylians, who had fought for the Carthaginians in Hispania, had been excluded from the kingship when he lost his father Gala.

[29.15]He had repeatedly tried to regain it by war, but had in several battles been defeated by king Syphax of Numidia, and had lost everything. As an exile he and two hundred cavalry joined Scipio, and with his help, Scipio defeated Hanno, the son of Hamilcar, together with many soldiers, right at the beginning of the war.

[29.16]When Hasdrubal, Syphax, and hundred thousand men approached, Scipio was forced to raise the siege of [Utica](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/utica/), and settle in a winter camp.

[29.17]Consul Sempronius successfully fought against Hannibal in the country of Croton.

[29.18]There was a remarkable quarrel between the two [censors](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/censor/) Marcus Livius and Claudius Nero.

[29.19]Because on the one hand, Claudius took away the [public] horse from his colleague because he had once been condemned and had been exiled by the people, and on the other hand Livius did the same to Claudius, because he had spoken falsely about him and had been insincere when they had been reconciled.

[29.20]He also registered all districts (except for one) as tax payers of the lowest order, because they had once condemned him, although he had been innocent and they had later made him consul and censor.

[29.21]The censors celebrated the _[lustrum](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/lustrum/)_ ceremony.

[29.22]214,000 citizens were registered.

### From Book 30

[30.1][203] In Africa, Scipio, aided by Massinissa, defeated the Carthaginians, the aforementioned king Syphax of Numidia, and Hasdrubal in several engagements, and captured two camps. Forty thousand people were killed by fire and fight.

[30.2]Syphax was captured by Gaius Laelius and Massinissa.

[30.3]Massinissa immediately fell in love with [Sophoniba](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/sophoniba/), the capive wife of Syphax and daughter of Hasdrubal, married her and had her as his wife; he was rebuked by Scipio, sent her poison, she drank it, and died.

[30.4]Because of Scipio's many victories, the desperate Carthaginians recalled Hannibal to protect the state.

[30.5][202] In the sixteenth year of his invasion of Italy, he withdrew, crossed to Africa and tried to organize a peace conference with Scipio, and when they could not agree about the peace conditions, he was defeated in battle.

[30.6]When the Carthaginians sued for peace, it was granted.

[30.7]When Gesco tried to dissuade the people from the peace, Hannibal pulled him down with his hand, apologized for his behavior, and argued for peace.

[30.8]Massinissa was given back his kingdom.

[30.9][201] After he had returned to the city, Scipio celebrated a very large and distinguished triumph, followed by the senator Quintus Terentius Culleo, who wore a liberty cap

[30.10]It is unclear whether Scipio received the surname _Africanus_ from his popularity with the soldiers or from the fickle favor of the people,

[30.11]but he certainly was the first commander to receive a surname derived from the conquered nation.

[30.12]In the country of the Insubres, Mago was wounded in a war against the Romans, was recalled to Africa by envoys, but died from his wound during the return voyage.

It was now the sixteenth year of the Punic War. The new consuls, Cnaeus Servilius and Caius Servilius, laid before the senate the questions of the general policy of the republic, the conduct of the war and the assignment of the provinces. It was resolved that the consuls should come to an arrangement, or failing that decide by ballot, which of them should oppose Hannibal in Bruttium whilst the other should have Etruria and the Ligurians as his province. The one to whom Bruttium fell was to take over the army from P. Sempronius, and Sempronius, whose command was extended for a year as proconsul, was to relieve P. Licinius; the latter was to return to Rome. Licinius was not only a fine soldier but he was in every respect one of the most accomplished citizens of the time; he combined in himself all the advantages which nature or fortune could bestow; he was an exceptionally handsome man and possessed remarkable physical strength; he was considered a most eloquent speaker, whether he was pleading a cause or defending or attacking a measure in the senate or before the Assembly, and he was thoroughly conversant with pontifical law. And his recent consulship had established his reputation as a military leader. Arrangements similar to those in Bruttium were also made in Etruria and Liguria; M. Cornelius was to hand over his army to the new consul and hold the province of Gaul with the legions which L. Scribonius had commanded the previous year. Then the consuls balloted for their provinces; Bruttium fell to Caepio, Etruria to Servilius Geminus. The balloting for the praetors' provinces followed; Aelius Paetus obtained the City jurisdiction, P. Lentulus drew Sardinia, P. Villius Sicily, and Quintilius Varus Ariminum with the two legions which had formed Lucretius Spurius' command. Lucretius had his command extended for a year to allow of his rebuilding Genua, which had been destroyed by Mago. Scipio's command was extended until the war in Africa was brought to a close. A decree was also made that, as he had entered upon his province of Africa, solemn intercessions should be offered up that the expedition might be to the advantage of the Roman people, of the general himself and of his army.

3000 men were raised for service in Sicily, as all the troops in that province had been taken to Africa and it had been decided that Sicily should be protected by forty ships until the fleet returned from Africa. Villius took with him thirteen new ships, the rest were the old ones in Sicily which were refitted. M. Pomponius, who had been praetor the year before, was appointed to take charge of this fleet, and placed on board the new levies he had brought from Italy. A fleet of equal strength was assigned to Cnaeus Octavius, who also had been praetor the previous year and was now invested with similar powers for the protection of the Sardinian coast. The praetor Lentulus was ordered to furnish 2000 men for service with the fleet. In view of the uncertainty as to where the Carthaginian fleet would land, though they would be sure to seek some unguarded spot, M. Marcius was furnished with forty ships to watch the coast of Italy. The consuls were authorised by the senate to raise 3000 men for this fleet and also two legions to defend the City against all contingencies. The province of Spain was left in the hands of the former commanders, L. Lentulus and L. Manlius Acidinus, who retained their old legions. Altogether there were 20 legions and 160 ships of war on active service this year. The praetors were ordered to go to their respective provinces. Before the consuls left the City they received the commands of the senate to celebrate the Great Games which the vow of the Dictator T. Manlius Torquatus required to be celebrated every five years, if the condition of the republic remained unaltered. Numerous stories of portents filled men's minds with superstitious terrors. It was said that crows picked with their beaks some of the gold on the Capitol and actually ate it, and rats gnawed a golden crown at Antium. The whole of the country round Capua was covered by an immense flight of locusts, and no one knew whence they had come. At Reate a foal was born with five feet; at Anagnia fiery meteors were seen in different parts of the sky and these were followed by a huge blazing torch; at Frusino a thin bow encircled the sun, which afterwards grew to such a size that it extended beyond the bow; at Arpinum there was a subsidence of the ground and a vast chasm was formed. Whilst one of the consuls was sacrificing, the liver of the first victim was found to be without a head. These portents were expiated by sacrifices of full-grown animals, the college of pontiffs intimated the deities to whom they were to be offered.

When this business was completed the consuls and praetors departed to their various provinces. They were all, however, interested in Africa, as much so indeed as if the ballot had assigned it to them, whether it was that they saw that the issue of the war and their country's fate would be decided there, or that they wished to do a service to Scipio as the man to whom all eyes were turned.
