**Numidia**, under the [Roman Republic](https://www.britannica.com/place/Roman-Republic) and Empire, a part of [Africa](https://www.britannica.com/place/Africa) north of the [Sahara](https://www.britannica.com/place/Sahara-desert-Africa), the boundaries of which at times corresponded roughly to those of modern western [Tunisia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Tunisia) and eastern [Algeria](https://www.britannica.com/place/Algeria). Its earliest inhabitants were divided into tribes and clans. They were physically indistinguishable from the other [indigenous](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/indigenous) inhabitants of early [North Africa](https://www.britannica.com/place/North-Africa) and, at the end of the [Roman Empire](https://www.britannica.com/place/Roman-Empire), were often categorized as [Berbers](https://www.britannica.com/place/Berbera). From the 6th century bce points along the coast were occupied by the [Carthaginians](https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia), who by the 3rd century bce had expanded into the interior as far as [Theveste](https://www.britannica.com/place/Tebessa) (Tébessa). Numidian [cavalry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/cavalry) was frequently found in the Carthaginian armies by that time.

The inhabitants remained seminomadic until the reign of [Masinissa](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Masinissa), the chief of the Massaesyli tribe, which lived near Cirta ([Constantine](https://www.britannica.com/place/Constantine-Algeria)). During the [Second Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/Second-Punic-War), he was initially an ally of Carthage, but he went over to the Roman side in 206 bce and was given further territory, extending as far as the Mulucha ([Moulouya](https://www.britannica.com/place/Moulouya-River)) River. The Romans under [Scipio Africanus](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Scipio-Africanus) and Numidians under Masinissa burned the camp of the rival Numidian chief [Syphax](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Syphax) near [Utica](https://www.britannica.com/place/Utica-Tunisia) and then overwhelmed Syphax and his Carthaginian allies at the Battle of Bagrades in 203 bce. Syphax had been wooed by [Rome](https://www.britannica.com/place/Rome), but his [allegiance](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/allegiance) to Carthage was cemented when he married Sophonisba, the daughter of the Carthaginian commander [Hasdrubal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hasdrubal-Carthaginian-general-died-circa-202-BCE). Syphax was captured and exiled to Rome, where he died at Tibur (modern [Tivoli](https://www.britannica.com/place/Tivoli-Italy)). Masinissa wished to claim Sophonisba as a wife, but when Scipio demanded that she go to Rome as a captive, Masinissa gave her poison so that she might escape the fate of a prisoner. (That tragic event was often depicted in later [Western paintings](https://www.britannica.com/art/Western-painting).)

Numidian [horsemanship](https://www.britannica.com/topic/horsemanship), [animal breeding](https://www.britannica.com/science/animal-breeding), and cavalry tactics eventually contributed to later developments in Roman [cavalry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/cavalry). In his history of Rome, [Polybius](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Polybius) underscores how important those cavalry advantages were to the outcome of the [Second Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/Second-Punic-War). Numidian superiority was demonstrated by the cavalry leadership of [Maharbal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Maharbal) under [Hannibal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hannibal-Carthaginian-general-247-183-BCE) at Trasimene and [Cannae](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Cannae) and later by Masinissa at [Zama](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Zama-Roman-Carthaginian-history) under Scipio Africanus. For nearly 50 years Masinissa retained the support of Rome as he tried to turn the Numidian pastoralists into peasant farmers. He also seized much Carthaginian territory and probably hoped to rule all of [North Africa](https://www.britannica.com/place/North-Africa).

On Masinissa’s death in 148 bce, the [Romans](https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Rome) prudently divided his kingdom among several chieftains, but the progress of civilization among the Numidians was not seriously interrupted, and, indeed, after 146 bce it received new [impetus](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/impetus) as thousands of Carthaginians fled to Numidia after the destruction of [Carthage](https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia). In 118 [Jugurtha](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Jugurtha), an [illegitimate](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/illegitimate) Numidian prince, usurped the throne and forcibly reunified Numidia until the Romans again took control in 105. Rome continued to dominate Numidia through client kings, though Numidian territory was considerably reduced. The third and final attempt by a Numidian to found a powerful state was that of [Juba I](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Juba-I), between 49 and 46 bce, ending with his defeat by [Julius Caesar](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Julius-Caesar-Roman-ruler) at [Thapsus](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Thapsus).

Caesar formed a new province, Africa Nova, from Numidian territory, and [Augustus](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Augustus-Roman-emperor) united Africa Nova (“New Africa”) with Africa Vetus (“Old Africa,” the [province](https://www.britannica.com/topic/province-ancient-Roman-government) surrounding Carthage), but a separate province of Numidia was formally created by [Septimius Severus](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Septimius-Severus). The Roman army’s Third Legion took up its permanent station at Lambaesis ([Lambessa](https://www.britannica.com/place/Lambessa)), and, as a result of the increased security, the Numidians’ population and prosperity increased substantially during the first two centuries ce. A few native [communities](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/communities) achieved municipal status, but the majority of the population was little touched by Roman civilization.

Key People: [St. Augustine](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Augustine)[Lucius Apuleius](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Lucius-Apuleius)[Jugurtha](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Jugurtha)[Masinissa](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Masinissa)[Ptolemy of Mauretania](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ptolemy-of-Mauretania)_(Show more)_

Related Places: [Althiburos](https://www.britannica.com/place/Althiburos)[Algeria](https://www.britannica.com/place/Algeria)[ancient Rome](https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Rome)_(Show more)_

[See all related content](https://www.britannica.com/facts/Numidia)

Christianity spread rapidly in the 3rd century ce, but in the 4th century Numidia became the centre of the [Donatist movement](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Donatists). That schismatic Christian group was particularly strong among the Numidian peasantry, to whom it appealed as a focus of protest against deteriorating social conditions. After the [Vandal](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Vandal-Germanic-people) conquest (429 ce), Roman civilization declined rapidly in Numidia, and the native elements [revived](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/revived) to outlive in some places even the Arab conquest in the 8th century and to persist until modern times.

**Masinissa** (born _c._ 238 bc—died 148 bc) was the ruler of the North African kingdom of [Numidia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Numidia) and an ally of [Rome](https://www.britannica.com/place/Rome) in the last years of the [Second Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/Second-Punic-War) (218–201). His influence was lasting because the economic and political development that took place in Numidia under his rule provided the base for later development of the region by the Romans.

Masinissa was the son of the chieftain of a Numidian tribal group, the Massyli. Brought up in [Carthage](https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia), of which his father was an ally, he fought for Carthage against the Romans in Spain from 211 to 206. When the Carthaginians were defeated at Ilipa (near modern Sevilla) by Scipio in 206, Masinissa switched sides and promised to assist Scipio in the invasion of Carthaginian territory in Africa. Meanwhile, his father had died; the Romans thereafter supported his claim to the Numidian throne against [Syphax](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Syphax), pro-Carthaginian ruler of the Massaesyli tribe. Syphax was successful in driving Masinissa from power until Scipio invaded Africa in 204. Masinissa joined the Roman forces and participated in the victorious [Battle of the Great Plains](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-the-Great-Plains), after which Syphax was captured. His Numidian [cavalry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/cavalry) were essential in Scipio’s victory at [Zama](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Zama-Roman-Carthaginian-history), which ended the Second Punic War and Carthage’s power.

After the defeat of Syphax and the Carthaginians, Masinissa became [king](https://www.britannica.com/topic/king-monarch) of both the Massyli and the Massaesyli. He showed unconditional loyalty to Rome, and his position in Africa was strengthened by a clause in the peace treaty of 201 between Rome and Carthage prohibiting the latter from going to war even in self-defense without Roman permission. This enabled Masinissa to [encroach](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/encroach) on the remaining Carthaginian territory as long as he judged that Rome wished to see Carthage weakened.

Masinissa’s chief aim was to build a strong and unified state from the seminomadic Numidian tribes. To this end he introduced Carthaginian agricultural techniques and forced many Numidians to settle as peasant farmers. Any hopes he may have had of extending his rule across [North Africa](https://www.britannica.com/place/North-Africa) were dashed when a Roman commission headed by the elderly [Marcus Porcius Cato](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Marcus-Porcius-Cato-Roman-statesman-234-149-BCE) came to Africa about 155 to decide a territorial dispute between Masinissa and Carthage. Animated probably by an irrational fear of a Carthaginian revival, but possibly by suspicion of Masinissa’s ambitions, Cato thenceforward advocated, finally with success, the destruction of Carthage. Masinissa showed his displeasure when the Roman army arrived in Africa in 149, but he died early in 148 without a [breach](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/breach) in the alliance.

**Second Punic War**, second (218–201 bce) in a series of wars between the [Roman Republic](https://www.britannica.com/place/Roman-Republic) and the Carthaginian (Punic) empire that resulted in Roman [hegemony](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/hegemony) over the western Mediterranean.

In the years after the [First Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/First-Punic-War), Rome wrested Corsica and [Sardinia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Sardinia-island-Italy) from [Carthage](https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia) and forced Carthaginians to pay an even greater indemnity than the payment exacted immediately following the [war](https://www.britannica.com/topic/war). Eventually, however, under the leadership of [Hamilcar Barca](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hamilcar-Barca), his son [Hannibal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hannibal-Carthaginian-general-247-183-BCE), and his son-in-law Hasdrubal, Carthage acquired a new base in [Spain](https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-Spain), whence they could renew the war against Rome.

In 219 Hannibal captured Saguntum (Sagunto) on the east coast of the [Iberian Peninsula](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iberian-Peninsula). Rome demanded his withdrawal, but Carthage refused to recall him, and Rome declared war. Because Rome controlled the sea, Hannibal led his army overland through Spain and [Gaul](https://www.britannica.com/place/Gaul-ancient-region-Europe) and across the Alps, arriving in the plain of the Po River valley in 218 bce with 20,000 [infantry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/infantry) and 6,000 [cavalry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/cavalry). Roman troops tried to bar his advance but were outmatched, and Hannibal’s hold over northern Italy was established. In 217 Hannibal, reinforced by Gallic tribesmen, marched south. Rather than attack Rome directly, he marched on [Capua](https://www.britannica.com/place/Capua-ancient-city-Italy), the second largest town in Italy, hoping to incite the populace to rebel. He won several battles but still refrained from attacking the city of Rome, even after [annihilating](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/annihilating) a huge Roman army at Cannae in 216. The defeat [galvanized](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/galvanized) Roman resistance. A brilliant defensive strategy conducted by Quintus Fabius Maximus [Cunctator](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Quintus-Fabius-Maximus-Verrucosus) harried the Carthaginians without offering battle. Thus, the two armies remained deadlocked on the Italian peninsula until 211 bce, when Rome recaptured the city of [Capua](https://www.britannica.com/place/Capua-Italy).

In 207 [Hasdrubal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hasdrubal-Carthaginian-general-died-207-BCE), following Hannibal’s route across the Alps, reached northern Italy with another large army supported by legions of Ligurians and Gauls. Hasdrubal marched down the peninsula to join Hannibal for an assault on Rome. Rome, exhausted by war, nevertheless raised and dispatched an army to check Hasdrubal. [Gaius Nero](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gaius-Claudius-Nero), commander of the southern Roman army, slipped away north also and defeated Hasdrubal on the banks of the Metauros River. Hannibal maintained his position in southern Italy until 203, when he was ordered to return to Africa. Italy was free of enemy troops for the first time in 15 years. During the long mainland campaign, fighting had continued as well on Sardinia and [Sicily](https://www.britannica.com/place/Sicily), which had become Rome’s chief sources of food. Aided by internal upheaval in [Syracuse](https://www.britannica.com/place/Syracuse-Italy), Carthage reestablished its presence on the island in 215 and maintained it until 210. Meanwhile, in Spain, Roman forces maintained pressure on Carthaginian strongholds. The Roman general [Publius Scipio](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Scipio-Africanus) won a decisive battle at Ilipa in 206 and forced the Carthaginians out of Spain.

 Quick Facts

Also called: Second Carthaginian War _(Show more)_

Date: 218 BCE - 201 _(Show more)_

Participants: [Carthage](https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia)[ancient Rome](https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Rome)_(Show more)_

Major Events: [Battle of Cannae](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Cannae)[Battle of Ilipa](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Ilipa)[Battle of Zama](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Zama-Roman-Carthaginian-history)[Battle of Trasimene](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-Trasimene)[Battle of the Trebbia River](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-the-Trebbia-River)_(Show more)_

Key People: [Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Quintus-Fabius-Maximus-Verrucosus)[Gaius Flaminius](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gaius-Flaminius)[Hannibal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hannibal-Carthaginian-general-247-183-BCE)[Masinissa](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Masinissa)[Gaius Claudius Nero](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gaius-Claudius-Nero)_(Show more)_

[See all related content](https://www.britannica.com/facts/Second-Punic-War)

After his Spanish victory Scipio determined to invade the Carthaginian homeland. He sailed for Africa in 204 and established a beachhead. The Carthaginian council offered terms of surrender but [reneged](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/reneged) at the last minute, pinning its hopes on one last battle. The massed Carthaginian army, led by Hannibal, was defeated at Zama. The Carthaginians accepted Scipio’s terms for peace: Carthage was forced to pay an indemnity and surrender its navy, and Spain and the Mediterranean islands were ceded to Rome.
